items.followUp: Draw and label a plant cell, and briefly describe the function of its nucleus.

rubric.why: Shows the nuclear envelope and its pores.
rubric.description: Draws a double-membraned nuclear envelope with pores.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when both the double membrane and pores are shown and labelled.

rubric.why: Identifies the material inside the nucleus and the chromatin network.
rubric.description: Shows and labels nucleoplasm and chromatin.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when both structures are shown and labelled.

rubric.why: Identifies the nucleolus as a distinct nuclear structure.
rubric.description: Shows and labels the nucleolus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a distinct, labelled nucleolus.

rubric.why: Explains the main structural arrangement of the nucleus.
rubric.description: Explains that the nucleus is enclosed by a double membrane and contains nucleoplasm, chromatin and a nucleolus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct structural explanation naming these components.

modelAnswer: Draw an oval nucleus enclosed by two membranes and show pores in the nuclear envelope.
Inside it, draw a nucleolus and a thread-like chromatin network in the nucleoplasm.
Label: nuclear envelope (double membrane), nuclear pores, nucleoplasm, chromatin and nucleolus.
The nucleus is enclosed by a double membrane with pores; its nucleoplasm contains chromatin and one or more nucleoli.

items.followUp: Compare the cell structure and nutrition of organisms in the kingdoms Fungi and Plantae.

rubric.why: States the defining cellular features of Monera.
rubric.description: Describes Monera as unicellular prokaryotes without a true nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the prokaryotic, unicellular nature of Monera.

rubric.why: Gives the basic features of Protista.
rubric.description: Describes most protists as unicellular eukaryotes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying Protista as eukaryotic and mostly unicellular.

rubric.why: Identifies the main cell-wall and nutrition features of fungi.
rubric.description: Describes fungi as eukaryotic, usually multicellular organisms with chitin cell walls that absorb food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the characteristic fungal wall and absorptive nutrition.

rubric.why: Distinguishes plants and animals by cell wall and mode of nutrition.
rubric.description: States that plants have cellulose cell walls and make food by photosynthesis, while animals lack cell walls and obtain food heterotrophically.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly distinguishing both kingdoms.

modelAnswer: Monera: organisms are unicellular and prokaryotic; they lack a true nucleus.
Protista: organisms are eukaryotic and mostly unicellular; some are autotrophic and others heterotrophic.
Fungi: organisms are eukaryotic, mostly multicellular, have chitin cell walls and absorb nutrients from their surroundings.
Plantae: organisms are multicellular eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls; most make food by photosynthesis.
Animalia: organisms are multicellular eukaryotes without cell walls; they obtain food by ingestion.

items.followUp: Explain how ATP and reduced NADP are formed during the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Identifies the initial capture of light energy by chlorophyll.
rubric.description: States that chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking chlorophyll with absorption of light.

rubric.why: Describes the splitting of water and release of oxygen.
rubric.description: Explains that light energy splits water into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for photolysis and oxygen release.

rubric.why: Describes the movement of excited electrons through carriers and energy release.
rubric.description: States that excited electrons pass along electron carriers, releasing energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for electron transport and energy release.

rubric.why: Identifies ATP production in the light reaction.
rubric.description: Explains that released energy is used to form ATP by photophosphorylation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing ATP formation.

rubric.why: Identifies the reduction of NADP using hydrogen and electrons.
rubric.description: States that NADP accepts electrons and hydrogen to form reduced NADP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing reduced NADP formation.

modelAnswer: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy in the thylakoid membranes.
Light energy splits water into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen; oxygen is released.
The excited electrons pass along electron carriers, releasing energy.
This energy is used to make ATP from ADP and phosphate; this process is called photophosphorylation.
NADP accepts electrons and hydrogen to form reduced NADP.

items.followUp: Describe how proteins are digested in the small intestine.

rubric.why: Identifies gastric secretions and the acidic conditions in the stomach.
rubric.description: States that gastric glands secrete gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for gastric juice secretion and the role or presence of hydrochloric acid.

rubric.why: Explains how the stomach's protein-digesting enzyme becomes active.
rubric.description: Explains that hydrochloric acid activates pepsinogen to pepsin.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the activation of pepsinogen.

rubric.why: Identifies the enzyme and its action on proteins.
rubric.description: States that pepsin digests proteins into smaller peptides or peptones.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct action of pepsin on proteins.

rubric.why: Explains how the stomach lining is protected from acid and enzymes.
rubric.description: States that mucus protects the stomach lining.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the protective role of mucus.

rubric.why: Describes mixing and the passage of stomach contents onward.
rubric.description: Explains that muscular churning mixes food with gastric juice to form chyme, which passes to the small intestine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for churning and formation or onward passage of chyme.

modelAnswer: Gastric glands in the stomach wall secrete gastric juice, which contains hydrochloric acid and enzymes.
Hydrochloric acid makes the stomach contents acidic and activates pepsinogen to pepsin.
Pepsin digests proteins into smaller peptides or peptones.
Mucus protects the stomach lining from the acid and digestive enzymes.
Muscular contractions churn food with gastric juice to form chyme, which then passes into the small intestine.

items.followUp: Explain how humidity and wind affect the rate of transpiration.

rubric.why: Explains the effect of light through stomatal opening.
rubric.description: States that light generally opens stomata and increases transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly connecting light, stomata and transpiration.

rubric.why: Explains the usual effect of higher temperature.
rubric.description: States that higher temperature increases evaporation and usually increases transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct temperature effect.

rubric.why: Explains the effect of moist air on the water-vapour gradient.
rubric.description: States that high humidity reduces the water-vapour gradient and lowers transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct humidity effect.

rubric.why: Explains how moving air affects water vapour around leaves.
rubric.description: States that wind removes moist air around leaves and generally increases transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct wind effect.

modelAnswer: Light generally causes stomata to open, so transpiration increases.
Higher temperature increases evaporation from leaf surfaces and usually increases transpiration.
High humidity reduces the difference in water-vapour concentration between the leaf and air, so transpiration decreases.
Wind removes moist air around the leaf, maintaining the water-vapour gradient and generally increasing transpiration.

items.followUp: Define population and give one example.

rubric.why: Defines a community as interacting populations of different species in one place.
rubric.description: Defines a community as populations of different species living together in the same habitat.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a definition including different species and a shared habitat.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of a community.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example, such as a pond community.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid community example.

modelAnswer: A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in the same habitat.
Example: a pond community, containing populations of plants, fish, insects and microorganisms.

items.followUp: Name one book written by Al-Asma'i about animals and identify the animal it discusses.

rubric.why: Recognizes Al-Asma'i's work studying and writing about animals.
rubric.description: States that Abdul Malik Asma'i made important contributions through the study of animals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying his zoological work.

rubric.why: Gives examples of the animals covered in his writings.
rubric.description: Names animals such as horses, camels, sheep or wild animals that he wrote about.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for at least one valid animal group.

modelAnswer: Abdul Malik Asma'i was an early Muslim scholar who studied animals and wrote books about them.
His writings included accounts of horses, camels, sheep and wild animals.

items.followUp: What causes itching and swelling at the site of an insect bite?

rubric.why: Identifies the saliva introduced during the mosquito bite as the trigger.
rubric.description: States that mosquito saliva enters the skin during the bite.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying saliva as the cause of the local reaction.

rubric.why: Explains the local reaction that produces the raised, itchy welt.
rubric.description: Explains that the body's response to the saliva causes local swelling and itching.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the body's reaction to swelling or welt formation and itching.

modelAnswer: When a mosquito bites, saliva enters the skin.
The body's reaction to the saliva causes local swelling and itching, producing a raised welt.
